s.en: Merge subtrees together and split repository into subtrees

syn: git subtree [<options>] -P <prefix> [-S[<keyid>]] add <local-commit> ⏎ git subtree [<options>] -P <prefix> [-S[<keyid>]] add <repository> <remote-ref> ⏎ git subtree [<options>] -P <prefix> [-S[<keyid>]] merge <local-commit> [<repository>] ⏎ git subtree [<options>] -P <prefix> [-S[<keyid>]] split [<local-commit>] ⏎ git subtree [<options>] -P <prefix> [-S[<keyid>]] pull <repository> <remote-ref> ⏎ git subtree [<options>] -P <prefix> [-S[<keyid>]] push <repository> <refspec>

o.en: Suppress unnecessary output messages on stderr.
Produce even more unnecessary output messages on stderr.
Specify the path in the repository to the subtree you want to manipulate. This option is mandatory for all commands.
GPG-sign commits. The keyid argument is optional and defaults to the committer identity; --no-gpg-sign is useful to countermand a --gpg-sign option given earlier on the command line.

Instead of merging the entire history from the subtree project, produce only a single commit that contains all the differences you want to merge, and then merge that new commit into your project. Using this option helps to reduce log clutter.
Specify <message> as the commit message for the merge commit.

When generating synthetic history, add <annotation> as a prefix to each commit message. Since we’re creating new commits with the same commit message, but possibly different content, from the original commits, this can help to differentiate them and avoid confusion.
After generating the synthetic history, create a new branch called <branch> that contains the new history. This is suitable for immediate pushing upstream. <branch> must not already exist.

If you use --rejoin, git subtree attempts to optimize its history reconstruction to generate only the new commits since the last --rejoin. --ignore-joins disables this behavior, forcing it to regenerate the entire history. In a large project, this can take a long time.
If your subtree was originally imported using something other than git subtree, its history may not match what git subtree is expecting.
After splitting, merge the newly created synthetic history back into your main project. That way, future splits can search only the part of history that has been added since the most recent --rejoin.
